narrative:
The model determined that you have a 75% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the model toward predicting failure. Both placed you at the very bottom of your class—second and first decile respectively—well below the average performance of students who were accepted. These low rankings strongly signaled to the model that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 41, your score sits noticeably above the average of accepted students (37). This gave the model some confidence you could succeed, yet it was not enough to overcome the negative impact of your class standing.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.5, upper-middle family income, full-time status, gender, and race played only minor roles. The model focused overwhelmingly on how you performed once you entered law school.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking key courses, seeking academic support, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. Strengthening your academic record will be the most direct way to change future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
